units.title: Set Theory
units.intro: A set is a well-defined collection. Roster {1,2,3} or rule {x | x>0}. Equal = same elements. Equivalent = same count. A⊆B if every of A is in B. Proper ⊂ if also A≠B. Union ∪ = in A or B. Intersection ∩ = in both. Complement A′ = in U but not A. Difference A−B = in A not B. Cartesian A×B = ordered pairs.

cards.title: 1.1 Methods of Specifying Sets
body: The notion of a set is basic in Mathematics.
George Cantor, (1845-1918) a German mathematician created set theory, a new area of Mathematics.
A set is a collection of well-defined objects called elements.
A = the set of natural numbers less than or equal to 7, i. e., A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7}, This means that 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 are elements of set A.
If the elements of a set A can all be listed, then the set is given by putting the letter A equal to a brace which includes all the elements of A in any order whatsoever.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If $$A = \{1, 2, 3\}$$ and $$B = \{x, y, z\}$$, how are these two sets related?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Check for Equality**
Equal sets must have identical elements. Since $$1, 2, 3$$ are numbers and $$x, y, z$$ are letters, $$A \neq B$$.

**Step 2: Check for Equivalence**
Equivalent sets must have the same number of elements ($$n(A) = n(B)$$).
$$n(A) = 3$$ and $$n(B) = 3$$. Since $$n(A) = n(B)$$, the sets are equivalent.

**Step 3: Final Result**
They are equivalent sets.

cards.title: Quick check

cards.why:
**Step 1: Solve the equation**
$$x^2 - 16 = 0 \implies x^2 = 16 \implies x = 4$$ or $$x = -4$$.

**Step 2: Apply the set constraints**
The definition specifies $$x \in \mathbb{N}$$ (natural numbers). Natural numbers include only positive integers ($$\{1, 2, 3, 4, \dots\}$$).

**Step 3: Filter the solutions**
Since $$-4$$ is not a natural number ($$-4 \notin \mathbb{N}$$), the only valid element is $$4$$.

**Step 4: Final Result**
Set $$A = \{4\}$$.

cards.title: Step by step: equal or equivalent?
body: **Equal sets (A = B):** exactly the same elements; order and repetition do not matter. {1, 2, 3} = {3, 1, 2} = {1, 1, 2, 3}.
**Equivalent sets (A ↔ B):** the same number of elements, n(A) = n(B), so they can be matched one-to-one. {a, b, c} ↔ {1, 2, 3}.

**How to decide:** Step 1: list both sets without repeats. Step 2: count the elements — different counts → neither equal nor equivalent. Step 3: same count → equivalent; if also the very same elements → equal.
Every pair of equal sets is equivalent, but equivalent sets need not be equal.

options.A: A and B are equivalent but not equal

cards.why: Listing the letters of "BOOK" without repetition gives A = {B, O, K}. B has exactly the same three elements (order does not matter), so A = B. Equal sets are of course also equivalent.

cards.title: Equal vs equivalent — with examples
body: **Equal sets** have exactly the same elements: {2, 4, 6} = {6, 2, 4} = {x : x is an even number, 0 < x < 8}. **Equivalent sets** (A ~ B) only need the same number of elements, n(A) = n(B), so their elements can be matched one-to-one.
{a, b, c} and {1, 2, 3} are equivalent but not equal. Every pair of equal sets is equivalent, but not every pair of equivalent sets is equal.
**Finite and infinite sets:** {1, 2, …, 100} is finite (n = 100); the set of natural numbers {1, 2, 3, …} is infinite. The empty set ∅ = { } has n(∅) = 0, and {0} is NOT empty (it has one element).

cards.title: Worked example: equal or equivalent?
cards.problem: A = {x : x is a letter of the word "LEVEL"}, B = {E, V, L}, C = {1, 2, 3}. Compare the sets.

steps.text: Step 1: list A without repeats: A = {L, E, V}.
Step 2: A and B contain exactly the same letters, so A = B.
Step 3: n(A) = 3 = n(C), so A ~ C (equivalent), but A ≠ C because the elements are different.

cards.answer: A = B; A and C are equivalent, not equal.

cards.title: 1.3 Subsets and Proper Subsets
body: Every set is a subset of itself, and the empty set is a subset of every set.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If $$A \subseteq B$$ and $$B \subseteq A$$, which of the following must be true?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze set definitions**
$$A \subseteq B$$ means every element of $$A$$ is in $$B$$.
$$B \subseteq A$$ means every element of $$B$$ is in $$A$$.

**Step 2: Draw mathematical conclusion**
When both statements are simultaneously true, the two sets must consist of identical elements. Thus, $$A = B$$.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, **$$A = B$$**.

cards.title: Step by step: subsets
body: A ⊆ B (A is a **subset** of B) means every element of A is also in B. A ⊂ B (**proper subset**) means A ⊆ B and B has at least one element that A does not have.
Facts: ∅ ⊆ A for every set A; A ⊆ A for every set A; but A is never a proper subset of itself.
**Counting subsets:** a set with n elements has **2ⁿ subsets** and **2ⁿ − 1 proper subsets**. Example: {a, b} has 2² = 4 subsets: ∅, {a}, {b}, {a, b}; 3 of them are proper.
**Tip:** to list all subsets of {1, 2, 3} systematically, list by size: ∅; {1}, {2}, {3}; {1, 2}, {1, 3}, {2, 3}; {1, 2, 3} — 8 subsets.

cards.title: Practice

cards.why: A set with n = 4 elements has 2⁴ = 16 subsets. All except the set itself are proper, so there are 16 − 1 = 15 proper subsets.

cards.title: Step by step: union and intersection
body: **A ∪ B** = all elements that are in A **or** B (or both). **A ∩ B** = elements in **both** A and B.
**Counting formula:** n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B). The overlap is subtracted once because it was counted twice. Check: 4 + 3 − 2 = 5 ✔.
**Word problem:** in a class of 40, 25 like football, 18 like volleyball and 8 like both. Students who like at least one = 25 + 18 − 8 = 35; students who like neither = 40 − 35 = 5.

cards.title: 1.5.1 Complement of a Set
body: A universal set is a set that contains all the elements being considered in a given discussion or problem.
The complement of set A is the set of all elements in the universal set that are not in A.
The complement of set A is denoted by A′.

cards.title: 1.5.2 Difference of Sets
body: The difference of a set A with respect to set B is the set of elements in B that are not in A.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define complement**
The complement $$A'$$ contains all elements in the universal set $$U$$ that are not in set $$A$$.

**Step 2: Exclude elements of $$A$$ from $$U$$**
$$U = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$$. Excluding $$2$$ and $$3$$ leaves $$\{1, 4, 5\}$$.

**Step 3: Final Result**
$$A' = \{1, 4, 5\}$$.

steps.text: The complement $$A'$$ contains all elements in the universal set $$U$$ that are not in set $$A$$.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define set difference**
$$A - B$$ is the set of elements that are in $$A$$ but not in $$B$$.

**Step 2: Analyze elements**
The elements in $$A$$ are $$a, b, c$$. The elements in $$B$$ are $$b, c, d$$. The only element that is in $$A$$ and not in $$B$$ is $$a$$.

**Step 3: Final Result**
$$A - B = \{a\}$$.

steps.text: $$A - B$$ is the set of elements that are in $$A$$ but not in $$B$$.
The elements in $$A$$ are $$a, b, c$$. The elements in $$B$$ are $$b, c, d$$. The only element that is in $$A$$ and not in $$B$$ is $$a$$.

cards.title: Step by step: complement and difference
body: The **universal set U** contains everything under discussion. The **complement** A′ (also written Aᶜ) is everything in U that is **not** in A. The **difference** A − B (also A \ B) is everything in A that is **not** in B.
Useful facts: A − B = A ∩ B′; n(A′) = n(U) − n(A); (A′)′ = A.
**De Morgan's laws:** (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ and (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′.

cards.title: Practice

For example if Saba is sitting in the 3rd column and 1st row, write S(3,1).
A pair of numbers in which x is the first and y is the second is called an ordered pair and is written as (x, y).
Since the order in which the numbers occur is considered as well as the numbers, it follows that (y, x) and (x, y) are different ordered pairs unless y = x.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Let $$A = \{1, 2\}$$ and $$B = \{a, b\}$$. What is the cardinality of $$A \times B$$?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall the product rule for cardinality**
$$n(A \times B) = n(A) \times n(B)$$.

**Step 2: Count elements of both sets**
$$n(A) = 2$$ and $$n(B) = 2$$.

**Step 3: Calculate the product**
$$n(A \times B) = 2 \times 2 = 4$$.

**Step 4: Final Result**
The cardinality is **$$4$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If $$A = \{3\}$$ and $$B = \{1, 2\}$$, what is $$A \times B$$?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Apply Cartesian product definition**
$$A \times B = \{(a, b) : a \in A \text{ and } b \in B\}$$.

**Step 2: Form ordered pairs**
Pair the single element $$3$$ from set $$A$$ with every element in $$B = \{1, 2\}$$.
Pairs are $$(3, 1)$$ and $$(3, 2)$$.

**Step 3: Final Result**
$$A \times B = \{(3, 1), (3, 2)\}$$.

cards.title: Step by step: Cartesian product
body: The **Cartesian product** A × B is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) with a ∈ A and b ∈ B. Order matters: (1, x) is not the same as (x, 1).
Example: A = {1, 2}, B = {x, y, z}. A × B = {(1, x), (1, y), (1, z), (2, x), (2, y), (2, z)}. Method: take each element of A in turn and pair it with every element of B.
**Counting:** n(A × B) = n(A) × n(B) = 2 × 3 = 6. In general A × B ≠ B × A (but they have the same number of elements).
A × B can be shown as a grid of points (lattice) — this is the idea behind the coordinate plane ℝ × ℝ.

cards.title: Practice
cards.q: If n(A) = 3 and n(A × B) = 15, how many elements does B have?
cards.why: n(A × B) = n(A) × n(B), so 15 = 3 × n(B) and n(B) = 5.

cards.title: Step by step: slope
body: The **slope** (gradient) m of a line measures its steepness: $$m = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$$.
Example: through (2, 1) and (5, 7): m = (7 − 1)/(5 − 2) = 6/3 = 2. Keep the same order of points in the top and the bottom.
**Meaning of the sign:** m > 0 rises to the right; m < 0 falls; m = 0 horizontal; vertical lines have undefined slope.
**Parallel and perpendicular:** parallel lines have equal slopes (m₁ = m₂); perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is −1 (m₁ · m₂ = −1), e.g. 2 and −½.

Since both equations are identical, they represent the same line.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The system has **infinitely many solutions**.

cards.title: 4.1 Representing a quadratic function
body: A **quadratic function** has the form $$f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$$ with a ≠ 0. Examples: f(x) = x², f(x) = 2x² − 3x + 1, the area of a square A(s) = s². Not quadratic: f(x) = 3x + 1 (no x² term) or f(x) = x³.

Like any function, a quadratic can be shown **in words, by a formula, by a table of values, or by a graph**. Example in words: "a ball is thrown up; its height after t seconds is 20t − 5t² metres" → h(t) = −5t² + 20t.

**Table of values for f(x) = x² − 4 (step by step):** choose x = −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3 → f(x) = 5, 0, −3, −4, −3, 0, 5. Notice the values repeat symmetrically around x = 0 — every quadratic table is symmetric about its axis.
**Identifying a, b and c:** write the function in the order x², x, constant. f(x) = 5 − 2x + 3x² becomes 3x² − 2x + 5, so a = 3, b = −2, c = 5. The constant c is always the y-intercept: f(0) = c.
**Test from a table:** in a quadratic table (equal steps in x) the second differences are constant. For x² − 4: 5, 0, −3, −4 → differences −5, −3, −1 → second differences 2, 2.

body: Step 1 — **direction:** a > 0 opens up, a < 0 opens down.
Step 2 — **axis and vertex:** x = −b/(2a); put this x into the function to get the y-coordinate of the vertex.
Step 3 — **y-intercept:** (0, c).

body: Start from the basic parabola **y = x²** (vertex (0, 0), opens up). Changing one number at a time changes the graph in a predictable way.

**Changing a in y = ax²:** a > 1 makes the parabola **narrower** (steeper), 0 < a < 1 makes it **wider**, and a negative a turns it **upside down** (opens downward). Example: y = 3x² is narrower than y = x²; y = ½x² is wider; y = −x² opens down.
**Changing k in y = x² + k:** the whole graph moves **up k units** (k > 0) or **down** (k < 0). y = x² + 3 has vertex (0, 3); y = x² − 2 has vertex (0, −2).
**Changing h in y = (x − h)²:** the graph moves **right h units** when h > 0 and left when h < 0. Careful: y = (x − 2)² moves RIGHT 2 (vertex (2, 0)); y = (x + 2)² moves LEFT 2 (vertex (−2, 0)).

**All together — vertex form y = a(x − h)² + k:** vertex (h, k), axis of symmetry x = h, shape and direction from a. Example: y = −2(x − 1)² + 4 has vertex (1, 4), opens downward, is narrower than y = x², and its maximum value is 4.
**Tip:** "inside the bracket moves sideways the opposite way; outside moves up and down the same way".

**Step 2: Apply to the expression**
$$\frac{7^6}{7^2} = 7^{6-2} = 7^4$$

**Step 3: Final Result**

cards.title: Pythagoras’ theorem and its converse
body: In a right-angled triangle with legs a, b and hypotenuse c (the side opposite the right angle, always the longest): **a² + b² = c²**.
**Finding a leg:** a = √(c² − b²). Example: hypotenuse 13, leg 5 → other leg √(169 − 25) = √144 = 12.
**Converse:** if a² + b² = c² for the sides of a triangle, the triangle is right-angled (the right angle is opposite c). If a² + b² > c² the largest angle is acute; if a² + b² < c² it is obtuse.
**Pythagorean triples:** 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25 and their multiples (6-8-10, 9-12-15).

cards.title: 6.3.2 Angle of Elevation and Angle of Depression
body: The **angle of elevation** is the angle between the horizontal line and your line of sight when you look **up** at an object (for example, from the ground up to the top of a tree). The **angle of depression** is the angle between the horizontal and your line of sight when you look **down** (for example, from a cliff down to a boat).
Because the horizontal lines at the observer and at the object are parallel, the angle of depression from A to B equals the angle of elevation from B to A (alternate angles).

**Example:** a rope supporting a flagpole is fixed to the ground 8 m from the foot of the pole and makes an angle of elevation of 60° with the ground. Find the height of the point where the rope is tied and the length of the rope.

**Solution:** the pole, the rope and the ground form a right-angled triangle. Height h is opposite the 60° angle and 8 m is adjacent: tan 60° = h/8, so h = 8 × √3 ≈ 13.9 m. The rope is the hypotenuse: cos 60° = 8/r, so r = 8 ÷ 0.5 = 16 m.

cards.title: Step by step: profit and loss
body: **Cost price (CP)** is what the seller paid; **selling price (SP)** is what the buyer pays. SP > CP → profit = SP − CP. SP < CP → loss = CP − SP.
**Percentages are on the cost price:** profit % = profit/CP × 100%; loss % = loss/CP × 100%.
Example: a trader buys a goat for 1600 Nakfa and sells it for 2000 Nakfa. Profit = 400; profit % = 400/1600 × 100% = 25%.

**Finding SP from a percentage:** SP = CP × (1 + p%) for a profit, CP × (1 − p%) for a loss. **Finding CP:** CP = SP ÷ (1 + p%). Example: sold for 1150 Nakfa at 15% profit → CP = 1150 ÷ 1.15 = 1000 Nakfa.

cards.title: The four operations on polynomials
body: **Add/subtract:** combine like terms (same variable, same power). (3x² − 2x + 5) − (x² + 4x − 1) = 3x² − 2x + 5 − x² − 4x + 1 = 2x² − 6x + 6. Change every sign in the bracket after a minus.

**Multiply:** multiply every term of the first polynomial by every term of the second, then collect like terms: (x + 3)(2x − 1) = 2x² − x + 6x − 3 = 2x² + 5x − 3. Special products: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b², (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b².
**Divide:** long division as with numbers — divide the leading terms, multiply back, subtract, bring down. Dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder.

Step 2 — **y-intercept:** the constant term.

Step 4 — a few **test values** between the zeros to see whether the graph is above or below the axis.
